TITLE: Diagnosis of Inter-modal Gradient Conflicts in AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the disagreement between text and vision gradients in a modality-shared AR transformer using a novel layer-wise analysis technique. We'll utilize a modified version of the saliency backpropagation method, designed specifically for multi-modal autoregressive models, to measure the strength of inter-modal gradient conflicts at different depths of the network. We'll analyze these conflicts on the popular COCO-VQA dataset and the text-to-image generation task on the COCO dataset.
CONTROLS: Compare against a strong vision-language baseline (e.g., CLIP) and a naive multi-modal AR model with identical depth and width, but without gradient counterfactuals and confusion as diagnosed for interactions.
COST: Estimated 100 GPU-hours for the analysis and experiments.
PREDICTION: We expect to identify a clear pattern of inter-modal conflicts being more pronounced in the final layers of the transformer, particularly in tasks that require generative capabilities. This should provide valuable insights into the statistical properties of text and images that lead to these conflicts.

I anticipate that our analysis will reveal a clear disagreement between text and vision gradients, especially in the later layers. However, validating the performance benefits of modality-aware adjustments to the learned representations is crucial for this investigation.

TITLE: Modality-Aware Layer Normalization for AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Introduce a modality-aware layer normalization (M-LN) technique that adaptively adjusts the normalization scale and shift for each modality (text and vision). This layer-specific adaptation mechanism learns to mitigate inter-modal conflicts by leveraging both modalities' correlation and mutual information. We'll implement M-LN on the diagnosis toolkit (Proposal 1) and evaluate its effectiveness in reducing gradient conflicts and improving performance on COCO-VQA and text-to-image generation.
CONTROLS: Compare against the original model, the model with the modified backbone learned after proposal 1's tools are used, and a naive M-LN with shared normalization parameters for both modalities.
COST: Estimated 200 GPU-hours, leveraging the findings from Proposal 1.
PREDICTION: By applying M-LN, we expect a significant reduction in inter-modal conflicts, as visual and text features will be better aligned, leading to improved gradient stability and enhanced multimodal understanding.

PROPOSAL: We'll revise Proposal 2 by adding a novel regularization term to the loss function that penalizes modality-inconsistent representations across different layers of the transformer. This term, dubbed "modality inconsistency penalty" (MIP), encourages the network to maintain consistent, modality-specific feature distributions throughout its depth, further reducing inter-modal conflicts. We'll evaluate the impact of MIP in conjunction with M-LN (Proposal 2) on COCO-VQA and text-to-image generation tasks.
CONTROLS: Preserve all existing baselines, adding a new comparison against the model with only M-LN (original proposal) and the model with only MIP (training without M-LN).

PREDICTION: The addition of MIP should enhance the effects of M-LN, leading to a more consistent alignment of modality-specific features. However, the extent of performance improvement depends on the delicate balance between regularizing modality consistency and preserving the natural feature exchange between modalities.

TITLE: Multi-Task Training for AR UMMs with Inter-Modal Modular Routing
PROPOSAL: We'll investigate the integration of multi-task learning and inter-modal modular routing (IMR) in AR UMMs. IMR is a mechanism that dynamically routes predictions between different transformer layers, allowing each layer to specialize in one modality or the other. By adding a new IMR branch, we aim to explore whether task-specific routing can alleviate inter-modal conflicts and improve overall model performance in COCO-VQA and text-to-image generation tasks.
CONTROLS: Compare against the model with M-LN (Proposal 2), the model with IMR without M-LN, and a variant of the IMR model that allows routing across both modalities.
COST: Estimated 300 GPU-hours, leveraging the initial findings from Proposals 1 and 2.
PREDICTION: We expect the IMR mechanism to provide structural support for modality-specific processing within the transformer, which could complement the inter-modal alignment facilitated by M-LN and exhibit improved performance on both VQA and image generation tasks.

Our goal is to provide a comprehensive system that overcomes the challenges of inter-modal conflicts and enables the development of robust and adaptable models for a wide range of vision-language tasks.

TITLE: Mitigating Inter-Modal Conflicts through Modality-Conditioning
PROPOSAL: Introduce a modality-conditioning strategy to adaptively adjust the attention patterns and representation refinement within individual transformer layers. This approach leverages modality-specific information to selectively enhance or suppress the impact of cross-modal gradients on the layer's output. Specifically, we use binary masks to gate the interaction between vision and text representations within each layer, learning to control the flow of inter-modal information. This strategy will be evaluated on multiple tasks, including text-to-image generation and visual question answering.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Shared AR transformer without modality-conditioning. Ablations: analyze the effectiveness of different modality-conditioning architectures (e.g., mask-based, embedding-based).
COST: 150 GPU-hours (moderate-scale transformer training with additional modality-conditioning mechanisms).
PREDICTION: We expect modality-conditioning to improve training efficiency and performance, but may observe degraded results if the conditioning strategy is overly restrictive or aggressive, potentially limiting the model's ability to capture key inter-modal relationships.

TITLE: Flexible Modality Fusion via Conditional Attention
PROPOSAL: Introduce a conditional attention mechanism that dynamically adjusts the way the shared transformer layers integrate information from the two modalities. This flexibility allows the model to selectively focus on one modality or the other when it is more relevant for a given task. The mechanism is conditional on a learned modality indicator that is informed by the sequence's semantic content. We investigate this design on a range of tasks and evaluate its ability to improve modality-shared model performance.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Shared AR transformer. Ablations: analyze the effect of varying attention weights, attention dimensionality, and modality indicator smoothing.
COST: 100 GPU-hours ( moderate-scale transformer training with additional conditional attention computations).
PREDICTION: We expect the conditional attention mechanism to adaptively align vision and language, leading to improved results on various tasks. However, it might introduce instability if the modality indicator is noisy or if the conditional attention weights are not properly regularized.

TITLE: Task-Agnostic Multi-Task Learning for AR UMMs
PROPOSAL: Introduce a task-agnostic multi-task learning framework for AR UMMs, allowing the model to learn a shared representation that can be adapted for various tasks. The approach involves sharing a set of spherical layers across tasks and having each task-specific head learning on top of the shared representation. To reduce inter-modality conflicts, we apply the modality-conditioning strategy (proposal 3) and flexible modality fusion mechanism (proposal 5) on the shared representation. We evaluate the framework on a diverse set of tasks.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Separate models for each task. Ablations: compare with and without modality-conditioning and flexible modality fusion.
COST: 230 GPU-hours (large-scale transformer training with multiple task-specific heads).
PREDICTION: We expect the task-agnostic multi-task learning framework to learn a robust shared representation that can be effectively adapted for various tasks, leading to improved performance and reduced inter-modality conflicts. However, the framework might require careful hyperparameter tuning to balance the sharing and adaptation of the shared representation.
